title: After being sidelined, Boeing's Starliner to get starring role in NASA's spaceflight plans
gist: With SpaceX signaling it will retire Crew Dragon by 2030 to pivot to Starship, Starlink and an orbital-data-center megaconstellation, NASA is expected to announce it will order two more crewed Starliner missions from Boeing, help fund fixes to Starliner's thruster problems, and help certify a new launch vehicle as the Atlas V retires with only six rockets left. The move rescues a program that has cost Boeing over $2 billion in charges and leaves NASA and private station operators facing a single, uncompeted crew provider.

insights.claim: Multiple sources confirmed that as early as next week NASA will announce it is ordering two additional crewed Starliner missions from Boeing, paying some of the costs to fix the spacecraft's thruster issues, and supporting certification of the spacecraft on a new rocket.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A near-term, concrete announcement that reverses Boeing's sidelining and commits federal money to a fixed-price program.
insights.locator: Multiple sources confirmed to Ars that as early as next week

insights.claim: The Commercial Crew program was structured as fixed-price, meaning contractors bear the cost of reaching certification, yet NASA will now provide undisclosed funding to Boeing to resolve propulsion system issues from Starliner's last two flights.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A departure from fixed-price discipline is a meaningful precedent for how NASA handles struggling commercial partners.
insights.locator: The Commercial Crew program was developed as a fixed-price program

insights.claim: Boeing has already taken in excess of $2 billion in charges because of its ongoing challenges with Starliner.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The scale of losses explains why Boeing might have exited, and why NASA support was the price of keeping it in.
insights.locator: Boeing has already taken in excess of $2 billion in charges

insights.claim: Since 2010, NASA has paid SpaceX approximately $3.1 billion and Boeing $5.1 billion for development and certification of their crew vehicles, yet SpaceX has flown 13 crewed ISS missions, all successful, while Boeing has flown none operationally.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A 65 percent cost premium for zero operational missions is the starkest available measure of the two programs' divergence.
insights.locator: NASA has paid SpaceX approximately $3.1 billion and Boeing $5.1 billion

insights.claim: SpaceX made clear to NASA officials in recent months that it intends to retire the Crew Dragon vehicle by 2030 if not before, and has begun publicly confirming a wind-down just six years after Dragon began flying humans.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Retiring a successful crew vehicle after six years signals that human LEO transport is not where SpaceX sees returns.
insights.locator: NASA is taking these steps after SpaceX made clear

insights.claim: SpaceX is pivoting to its much larger Starship rocket with the intent of launching its more lucrative Starlink satellites and a new megaconstellation focused on orbital data centers.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Orbital data centers as a named SpaceX priority is a notable strategic signal about where launch capacity will be directed.
insights.locator: the company is seeking to pivot toward its much larger Starship rocket

insights.claim: Asked on the All-In Podcast whether SpaceX would keep flying Crew Dragon to meet demand, President and COO Gwynne Shotwell declined to commit, saying only 'We're not retiring it today, for sure,' and argued Boeing should fly its own capsule because 'the government paid a lot of money for that.'
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A public refusal to commit from SpaceX's COO is what forced NASA's hand — watch for further Dragon timeline statements.
insights.quote: Boeing has been paid, I think, probably more than we have been paid to develop their human capsule. So we’re just gonna let them have some business.
insights.locator: Shotwell would not commit to that

insights.claim: Although NASA financially backed Dragon development, SpaceX has contractually fulfilled its obligations and can therefore do as it pleases with the vehicle, leaving NASA without leverage.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Fixed-price contracting means the government funds capability it cannot compel to continue — a structural lesson for public-private programs.
insights.locator: SpaceX has contractually fulfilled its obligations

insights.claim: Starliner experienced numerous issues on uncrewed test flights in 2019 and 2022, and most seriously, thruster problems nearly led to the catastrophic loss of two astronauts during its first crewed test flight in June 2024.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The near-loss-of-crew event is the reason NASA funding for fixes is being framed as a safety necessity.
insights.locator: Starliner experienced numerous issues on uncrewed test flights

insights.claim: In February NASA formally classified the 2024 Starliner crewed flight as a 'Type A' mishap, and astronauts Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams ultimately had to be returned to Earth on a Crew Dragon vehicle.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The highest mishap classification plus a rival-vehicle rescue is the record NASA is now electing to build on.
insights.locator: in February, NASA formally classified the 2024 flight of Starliner

insights.claim: New NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman wrote that Starliner 'has design and engineering deficiencies that must be corrected,' but that the most troubling failure was not hardware — it was 'decision-making and leadership that, if left unchecked, could create a culture incompatible with human spaceflight.'
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The administrator publicly assigning blame to NASA's own culture, not just Boeing, is a notable institutional admission.
insights.quote: It is decision-making and leadership that, if left unchecked, could create a culture incompatible with human spaceflight.
insights.locator: Isaacman wrote in a letter to the NASA workforce

insights.claim: NASA released a 311-page report on mistakes made by both Boeing and NASA, yet half a year later is returning to Boeing for a central role in its human spaceflight program.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The gap between the investigative findings and the procurement decision is the core tension in the story.
insights.locator: NASA released a 311-page report

insights.claim: Starliner's Atlas V rocket, assembled by United Launch Alliance but using Russian engines, is near retirement with only six rockets left — one for the uncrewed Starliner 1 test flight and five for subsequent crewed missions.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A hard count of six remaining rockets sets a firm deadline for re-certifying Starliner on a new booster.
insights.locator: The Atlas V rocket, assembled by United Launch Alliance

insights.claim: There will likely be a competition for Starliner's new launch vehicle that almost certainly comes down to United Launch Alliance's Vulcan and Blue Origin's New Glenn.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A two-horse race with NASA paying certification costs is a concrete near-term contract opportunity to track.
insights.locator: There will likely be a competition for a new launch vehicle

insights.claim: If Boeing flies Starliner on New Glenn, it would essentially give Blue Origin a free human-rating certification of its rocket — normally a costly, time-consuming process — plus a crew launch arm and facilities Blue Origin could reuse for its own Space Vehicle.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The second-order prize for Blue Origin dwarfs the launch contract itself — a subsidized path to crewed flight.
insights.locator: Were Boeing to decide to fly Starliner on New Glenn

insights.claim: The more powerful New Glenn could potentially launch a crewed spacecraft and a cargo vehicle such as Northrop's Cygnus into orbit simultaneously, saving launch costs, a dual-payload capability Vulcan may not have.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Dual-manifest capability could be the decisive economic argument for commercial station operators controlling costs.
insights.locator: the more powerful New Glenn rocket may also have another benefit

themes.theme: Market structure and the monopoly risk

insights.claim: In July, companies developing private space stations were panicking because SpaceX would not bid on crew transportation and Boeing would not commit to a price for the 2030s, leaving them building stations with no way to get people there or back.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Crew transport, not the station hardware, is the binding constraint on the entire commercial LEO economy.
insights.locator: panic was setting in among companies seeking to develop private space stations

insights.claim: NASA's action gives private station operators security that at least one crew provider will exist, but the lack of competition raises pricing concerns — the author asks pointedly, 'Will Boeing be a considerate monopolist?'
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Sole-source crew transport pricing is the key variable for commercial station business models after ISS retirement.
insights.quote: Will Boeing be a considerate monopolist?
insights.locator: although the lack of competition raises some pricing concerns

insights.claim: Blue Origin has had a dedicated team working for several years on a crewed 'Space Vehicle' to launch on New Glenn, with fairly advanced design work and some parachute drop tests completed, but it remains likely years and billions of dollars from spaceflight.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A third crew provider exists on paper but cannot relieve the 2030 gap — hence NASA's reliance on Boeing.
insights.locator: Blue Origin has had a dedicated team working on a crewed “Space Vehicle”

insights.claim: NASA could have opened a new competition to Boeing, Blue Origin and wild cards such as The Exploration Company for 2030s crewed missions, but appears to have had no appetite for the cost so soon after the Commercial Crew competition a decade ago.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Avoiding a new competition locks in the incumbent structure for a decade — the choice that creates the monopoly risk.
insights.locator: The space agency could have opened a new competition

insights.claim: The author suggests NASA may be meeting Boeing halfway because Boeing might otherwise have abandoned Starliner given its financial losses, adding that 'it also helps that Boeing has excellent lobbyists.'
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Political economy, not just capability, is being named as a factor in the procurement outcome.
insights.quote: It also helps that Boeing has excellent lobbyists.
insights.locator: So it’s possible that NASA is meeting Boeing halfway
